tagline.text: A quiet three-tier waterfall in a remote barangay of Monkayo, Davao de Oro

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Awao, Monkayo, Davao de Oro

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Best in the dry season (mostly March–May); avoid right after heavy rain

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,000 (per person from Monkayo; estimate including motorcycle charter, entrance fee, guide tip and one night's lodging)

children.text: Awao Falls is a three-tier waterfall in Barangay Awao, Monkayo. The largest, the first tier, is about 80 feet high and has a pool for swimming. It is a remote spot that requires a motorcycle ride and a stream crossing once the paved road ends.
Awao Falls is a waterfall in Barangay Awao, Monkayo, in the province of Davao de Oro, which used to be called Compostela Valley. According to Wikipedia, Monkayo lies about
120km
from Davao City by road and about
30km

from the provincial capital, Nabunturan. Wikipedia lists the Seven Falls of Awao among the area's sights and describes cold water, moss-covered rocks around the falls and a modest flow. Travel blogs describe three tiers in a row, and mention a possible fourth tier upstream, but none has been confirmed by photos.
What sets this place apart from better-known waterfalls is the way you reach it. The road from Monkayo town to the village at the entrance is rough, and travel blogs give times ranging from about
30 minutes
to more than
1 hour
. There is a shallow stream or river to cross on the way, and a 2014 blog says it took about
15 minutes
more on foot after the crossing. This is therefore a place for adventurous travelers rather than an easy sightseeing stop.
The first tier is reported to be about 80 feet high, and the pool below is said to be good for swimming. The second tier is described as about
high, and some accounts mention a few open cottages there. The third tier is said to be about
with a shallow natural pool. Heights differ a little from source to source, so confirm the details locally.

Facilities are basic. A trip report from March 2026 mentions a few concrete seats and tables and says only one other group was there. That makes for a quiet visit, but do not expect shops or amenities. Bring water, snacks, a change of clothes and a plastic bag. The prices and travel times in this guide are compiled from trip reports written between 2014 and 2026 and may have changed, so ask the Monkayo tourism office or the Barangay Awao office for current information before you go.

This is the tallest and largest of the falls, reported at about 80 feet. A pool collects the water below, and many visitors say it is good for swimming. The water is said to stay cold even in the dry season.
Beyond the first tier, a second and a third tier follow. The second is described as about
with open cottages, and the third as about
with a shallow pool. A fourth tier is only a rumor, with no photos.
You reach the falls from Monkayo by motorcycle. Locally, a motorcycle with an extended seat is sometimes called a skylab. Passing through countryside and villages is part of the trip.
On the way you cross a stream or river and walk part of the route. Warnings say the crossing is impassable after heavy rain, so be sure to check how high the water is.
Reviews say there are few visitors, so you can enjoy the falls in peace. A 2016 blog wrote that local residents hope to attract more tourists.
Guides for the falls have been arranged through the barangay. Walking with a local helps a great deal with route-finding and safety.
Wikipedia notes that Monkayo also has Kumbilan Cave and several waterfalls besides Awao. If you have time, you can give Awao one day and the other attractions another.

items.title: Two days in Monkayo
items.subtitle: Travel the day before, falls the next day

children.text: Travel from Davao to Monkayo. The bus or van takes about
3 hours
. Check into your lodging and agree on the next day's plan and fare with a motorcycle driver in advance.
Eat breakfast and set off by motorcycle from near the Monkayo terminal. If you can, go with 3–4 people in your group so you can share the fare.
Arrive at Barangay Awao, pay the entrance fee at the office or entrance, and talk with your guide. Ask about the stream conditions as well.
Cross the stream and walk to the falls. See the first tier first and swim, then look around the second-tier area.
Eat the lunch you brought, and plan to head back to Monkayo before it rains.
Back in Monkayo, shower and rest. If you have time left, look around town, then travel to Davao the next day.
Travel times and trail conditions differ from report to report, so the times above are only an example. Adjust them with your guide on site.
Take a Butuan-bound bus from the Davao Ecoland Terminal to Monkayo. It takes about
3 hours
Find a motorcycle driver at the Monkayo terminal and head for the falls.
Arrive at the falls, stay at the first tier and swim. If you want to go further, agree on the time with your guide.
After lunch, hurry back to Monkayo.
Check the last bus time to Davao and board. The return can run late, so leave yourself margin.
The round trip from Davao takes about 6–7 hours on the road, so it is hard to enjoy the falls fully in one day. One night in Monkayo is recommended if possible.
There are direct flights from Manila to Davao International Airport (DVO), taking about
2 hours
. Airlines and schedules change often, so check the latest timetable before booking.
You can also fly into Butuan and come south toward Monkayo. Take a Davao-bound bus from Butuan and get off at Monkayo; one blog gives about
3.5–4 hours
Flights can change, so check the latest announcements.
From the Davao Ecoland Terminal, take a Butuan-bound bus or van and get off at Monkayo. It takes about
3 hours
. Tell the driver or conductor that you are getting off at Monkayo.

From Monkayo town to the falls, charter a motorcycle (skylab) or a tricycle. Records from 2014 and 2016 show about

The ride takes around
1 hour
and includes a stream crossing. A 2026 report says the engine stalled at the stream and the traveler waited several hours, so leave room in your schedule.
As an alternative, a 2016 post describes sharing rides in stages: a bus from Monkayo to Santa Josefa for about
, a motorcycle to Awao village for about
, and a motorcycle toward the falls for about
Fares depend on the season and on negotiation.
Some guides recommend an SUV because the road is rough. They say renting a car in Davao cuts the travel time, but check the condition of the road locally once the pavement ends.
Monkayo's average daytime high is about
and the nighttime low about

. Wikipedia (Meteoblue model) gives annual rainfall of about 1,757mm and about 268 rainy days a year, but other climate datasets show 2,800mm or more, so treat these figures as a rough guide. It can rain at any time of year, so even in the dry season be ready for afternoon showers.

At this waterfall, road and stream conditions matter more than the weather. A 2014 blog warns that the road turns to mud in the rainy season and the stream cannot be crossed during flash floods. Avoid the day of heavy rain and the day after.

There is almost no lodging near the falls, so most people stay in Monkayo town. Trip reports show air-conditioned rooms from about ₱600 up to ₱1,500, and in 2026 an air-conditioned room at a place called Golden Inn was about ₱1,500. Prices change, so confirm before you arrive.

Eat in Monkayo town and bring a packed lunch and water to the falls. Nothing is known about whether there is a shop along the falls route. If you return to Davao or continue touring, you will eat at restaurants around the terminal.
Before you leave, contact the Barangay Awao office or Monkayo city hall to check the stream conditions and arrange a guide. A 2014 blog said prior coordination with the barangay is a must.
Agree with the motorcycle driver on the round-trip fare, waiting time and number of passengers first. Going with 3–4 people reduces the burden.
The suggested order is to see the first tier before climbing to the second. The path can be slippery, so wear shoes with good grip.
Bring a bag that can get wet or a waterproof pouch, a towel, a change of clothes and drinking water. Phone signal may be weak.
Carry plenty of cash. You pay the entrance fee, the motorcycle and the tip in cash.
Some reviews say the motorcycle back seat is rough and tiring on a long ride. Ask for a helmet and respect the passenger limit.
Plan to be back in Monkayo before dark. Leaving the falls around 2 p.m. is recommended.
Fees and trail conditions change from year to year, so check recent reviews and ask local people.
After rain the stream swells and cannot be crossed, and the road turns to mud. If heavy rain is forecast or has fallen recently, postpone your trip.
The only way to the third tier is by climbing the second tier itself, and reviews say the current below is strong. A slip could cause serious injury, so do not push yourself.
A 2016 report says debris left by past typhoons (Pablo in 2012 and Sendong in 2011) blocked the old trail to the first tier. Use only the route your guide shows you.
When swimming, check the depth and the rocks. No rescue facilities are known, and weak signal makes it hard to call for help.
Motorcycles are sometimes overloaded. Ride only within a safe limit.
Monkayo is a gold-mining area, so respect local guidance on the way and do not enter places that are not designated.
A cave in the Casoon area of Monkayo, known for stalactites and bats. Ask the city hall about its current condition and access.
A large waterfall in Cateel, Davao Oriental, and one of the best-known falls in the Davao region. It lies in a different direction from Awao, so plan it as a separate trip.
The gateway city for this region, with the airport and the Ecoland Terminal. It is a base for before and after your Monkayo trip.
Wikipedia also lists Sagay Falls and Pasian Falls. Check their condition and access locally.
